title: Internal Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with Noise
claim: Common validity indices mis-rank clusterings, favoring wrong shapes or noisy assignments, while ours ranks correct clusterings higher.
layout: 4 scatter panels in a row, paired comparisons, index scores under each
description: A single row of four 2-D scatter plots, each in a thin gray frame, with captions underneath listing three metric scores (DISCO, SC, DBCV). Panels (a) and (b) show concentric rings: (a) is the ground truth, with a red inner ring, a blue middle ring and a yellow-green outer ring, plus sparse gray plus-sign noise. (b) is a k-Means result that cuts across the rings, so each ring is split into red, blue and yellow-green arcs. Panels (c) and (d) show two ring-shaped clusters, one red and one blue, surrounded by many gray noise crosses. In (c) the rings are clean. In (d) some noise points have been absorbed into the clusters as colored dots inside and around the rings. The score lines show DISCO agreeing with the intuitive ranking while SC or DBCV prefer the worse clustering. The eye goes first to the colorful rings.
caption: Ring-shaped ground truth clusters (color-coded) with noise (gray \textcolor{gray}{{ +}}). Top: The density-based CVIs DISCO and DBCV rate the ground truth ring clustering in (a) higher than the $k$-Means clustering cutting across rings in (b), while the Silhouette Coefficient (SC) prefers the latter. Bottom: DISCO scores the "clean" clustering in (c) higher than the version where some noise points are added to the ring-shaped clusters (d). DBCV only evaluates the amount of noise, and, thus, prefers the latter.
abstract: Being able to evaluate the quality of a clustering result even in the absence of ground truth cluster labels is fundamental for research in data mining. However, most cluster validation indices (CVIs) do not capture noise assignments by density-based clustering methods like DBSCAN or HDBSCAN, even though the ability to correctly determine noise is crucial for successful clustering. In this paper, we propose DISCO, a Density-based Internal Score for Clusterings with nOise, the first CVI to explicitly assess the quality of noise assignments rather than merely counting them. DISCO is based on the established idea of the Silhouette Coefficient, but adopts density-connectivity to evaluate clusters of arbitrary shapes, and proposes explicit noise evaluation: it rewards correctly assigned noise labels and penalizes noise labels where a cluster label would have been more appropriate. The pointwise definition of DISCO allows for the seamless integration of noise evaluation into the final clustering evaluation, while also enabling explainable evaluations of the clustered data. In contrast to most state-of-the-art, DISCO is well-defined and also covers edge cases that regularly appear as output from clustering algorithms, such as singleton clusters or a single cluster plus noise.
